events.text: Crews completed track installation for the extension. The province marked the milestone at its future northern terminus.
Revenue trains reached Highway 7 at Millway Avenue, giving Vaughan’s planned downtown a subway terminus and a link to the Viva bus rapidway.
SmartVMC Bus Terminal opened. An enclosed walkway linked York Region buses to the subway concourse and the Highway 7 rapidway.
The subway opened west of Jane Street beside Highway 407. Its regional bus terminal gave GO bus riders a transfer to the subway before reaching downtown Toronto.
GO bus routes serving York University’s Keele campus moved here. University-bound riders continued by subway to York University or Pioneer Village.
Contractors handed the station to the TTC for testing. The complex included twelve TTC bus bays on the Toronto side and five regional bays on the Vaughan side.
Passengers first boarded beneath Steeles Avenue, the Toronto–Vaughan boundary. Entrances served bus terminals on opposite sides of the municipal line.
Doors Open Toronto visitors toured the station months before the first passenger trains. The wing-shaped entrance was designed to direct daylight down into the concourse.
The station opened beneath the university commons. Its entrances face York Lanes and the Accolade East Building, placing the subway within walking distance of the lecture halls.
The extension brought subway service to Keele and Finch. A bus terminal and parking in the nearby hydro corridor connected the surrounding neighbourhoods.
Line 6 began carrying passengers between Finch West and Humber College, making this station an interchange.
Passengers began using subway platforms beneath the Barrie GO rail corridor. Entrance pavilions on opposite sides of the railway were laid out for interchange with GO trains.
Barrie line trains began stopping at the new GO station above the subway, opening the rail-to-rail transfer.
The one-stop extension beyond Wilson officially opened here under the name Downsview.
Downsview became Sheppard West ahead of the extension to Vaughan, distinguishing it from the new Downsview Park station.
Public rides began at the original Spadina line terminus. Its two-level bus terminal gathered suburban routes beside the new Wilson subway yard.
The extension to Downsview moved several bus routes farther north and Wilson’s overflow bus terminal closed.
Trains began serving the shopping centre beneath an arched glass roof. Michael Hayden’s Arc en Ciel used moving bands of coloured neon to respond to arriving and departing trains.
Subway commuter parking reopened beneath the east end of Yorkdale Shopping Centre, on three levels of the mall’s Parkade E.
The TTC completed the station’s accessibility retrofit, giving riders a step-free route to the subway.
The new station put bus connections above the Allen Road rail corridor. The artwork Spacing … Aerial Highways marked the Lawrence Avenue entrance.
The station elevator entered service, giving riders a step-free route to the subway platform.
The Spadina line opened through the Allen Road median. Rita Letendre’s coloured skylight, Joy, brought daylight into the concrete station.
Rita Letendre reinterpreted Joy for the replacement skylight. Colour sits between layers of glass in the new design, protecting it from the leaks that damaged the original.
Elevators entered service at Glencairn, providing step-free subway access.
The station opened as Eglinton West where trains emerge from the ravine tunnel into the Allen Road median. Gerald Zeldin depicted a Toronto streetcar on the platform walls.
The TTC renamed Eglinton West for the Cedarvale neighbourhood.
The first Line 5 passenger service added an east–west light rail transfer.
Streetcars and buses met the new subway at an underground loop. Gordon Rayner’s enamel mural Tempo was installed on the mezzanine.
Morning rush-hour trains that used to turn back here began running north to Glencairn before reversing direction.
The TTC completed the station’s accessibility improvements, giving riders a step-free connection to Line 1.
Passengers entered through curved glass enclosures at Spadina Road. James Sutherland’s floral mosaics link the platforms visually to the mezzanine.
New elevators made the underground station accessible to riders who had previously faced stairs or escalators.
The Bloor-Danforth subway introduced passenger service at Spadina Avenue.
The new Spadina line platforms opened near Lowther Avenue. A moving walkway through a long passage connected them to the existing station.
The TTC removed the moving walkway after maintenance problems. Riders continued to use the connecting passage on foot.
University Avenue trains first terminated on the upper level. A second level had already been built for the future east–west subway.
The lower platforms opened and some trains ran directly between the University and Bloor-Danforth lines during a six-month service trial.
The University subway opened beside the Royal Ontario Museum. North of the station, the track layout allowed for a future junction with the east–west subway.
The TTC unveiled columns modelled on objects in museum collections and a new treatment of the platform walls.
Trains began serving the Ontario legislature and hospital district. Engineers tunnelled this stretch to limit disturbance above ground.
The MaRS Centre entrance opened, linking the station to the research complex at College Street and University Avenue.
The station opened in the tunnelled section of the University subway. Its curved platform walls originally carried painted station names.
A new entrance at 480 University Avenue brought sheltered stairs and elevator access to the station. It became the TTC’s 45th accessible subway station.
University subway service reached Queen Street West near Osgoode Hall. The station belonged to a group named for local landmarks and districts.
Renovation exposed the original blue-on-yellow glass tiles behind later wall strips before new panels were installed.
The University extension opened its King Street West station, displaying the cross street beneath the station name.
New platform cladding recalled the original grey and blue colour scheme and restored the TTC lettering.
Toronto’s first subway ended here beneath Front Street. Inaugural trains arrived from Eglinton before the public began riding that afternoon.
The University extension turned the terminus into a through station, allowing trains to continue north to St George.
The subway opened below Yonge Street at King. Immediately south, trains rounded a sharp curve towards the platforms under Front Street at Union.
The TTC removed the original track crossover north of the station during rehabilitation.
Builders left space under the Yonge platforms for a proposed Queen streetcar subway. Two passenger passages crossed beneath the tracks around that space.
Traffic moved off Queen Street between Bay and Victoria so crews could build the Ontario Line station that will connect with the existing subway.
The station opened as Dundas. Shallow platforms had separate fare controls on each side and stairs directly to street level.
Dundas became TMU following a naming agreement with Toronto Metropolitan University.
The station opened with side platforms served by a shared mezzanine. A crossover just south of College let trains move between tracks.
Charles Pachter’s Hockey Knights in Canada placed Toronto and Montréal players opposite one another on the platform walls, near Maple Leaf Gardens.
Because the line ran east of Yonge Street, the TTC could put a bus terminal directly above the tracks. Passengers changed between buses and trains inside the paid area.
Elevators made the station accessible. A new entrance on Dundonald Street also gave riders a second way in from the neighbourhood.
The original station opened as Bloor. Stairs led from the subway to a sheltered streetcar transfer platform in the middle of Bloor Street.
Bloor-Danforth trains replaced the streetcar transfer with a subway interchange at Yonge Street.
Passengers descended from the street-level entrance to two open-air platforms. The bus terminal sat alongside the railway cutting.
In October, elevators entered service at the open-air station, connecting its platforms to the entrance on Crescent Road.
The original Yonge subway served the neighbourhood beside the former North Toronto railway station. Its compact entrance served walk-in riders without a bus terminal.
Elevators entered service, giving both subway platforms step-free access from the Shaftesbury Avenue entrance.
A mezzanine connected the subway to a surface terminal and a second entrance on Pleasant Boulevard. St Clair streetcars were reorganized to feed the new line.
The TTC removed the Rosehill track crossover immediately south of the station. Its location near the Pleasant Boulevard portal had allowed trains to change tracks.
A replacement crossover was in place by summer as part of preparations for automatic train control on Line 1.
Opening-day guests boarded the inaugural train here. The station had a third track to move trains into and out of the adjacent yard.
The TTC opened its headquarters above the station’s bus terminal.
The first Yonge subway ended at the former Eglinton streetcar facility. A large bus terminal linked the new railway to neighbourhoods farther north.
With the extension to York Mills carrying passengers, Eglinton became a through station.
Introductory service on Line 5 added an east–west light rail connection beneath Yonge and Eglinton.
The York Mills extension brought passengers to Lawrence and Yonge. Buses entered an underground terminal and ran on the left to serve a central island.
Two elevators opened a step-free path from the street to the concourse, underground bus terminal and subway platform.
The subway reached Hogg’s Hollow, becoming a temporary northern terminus. Builders diverted the west branch of the Don River during excavation.
By the end of the York Mills Centre development, local buses had moved below ground and regional GO buses had a terminal at street level.
The station opened as Sheppard when the Yonge subway extended north from York Mills to Finch.
The station acquired the name Sheppard-Yonge and stairs linking the original Yonge platform to the new Sheppard platforms.
Regular Sheppard subway service began between this interchange and Don Mills.
Construction began in June at the site then known as Park Home. Crews built around the existing tunnel while Yonge trains continued running.
The TTC officially opened an infill station between Sheppard and Finch, providing a subway entrance in North York’s civic centre district.
Finch became the northern Yonge terminus on the original subway’s twentieth anniversary. Land in the hydro corridor helped make room for commuter parking.
Rio Algom donated Krystyna Sadowska’s metal sculpture Rhythm of Exotic Plants to the TTC. Riders encounter the artwork on the station mezzanine.
